content.rendered:
Assistant Professor of Economics Ethan Struby at St. Olaf College was recently featured in Marketplace on the growing role of artificial intelligence (AI) investment in the economy.

In the article, the Bureau of Economic Analysis reported that “the U.S. economy grew at an annualized rate of 2.2 percent in the second quarter, an upward revision from the previous estimate of 1.5 percent.” 

Struby provided expert insight on how the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure is contributing to gross domestic product (GDP) growth. He explained that companies are building data centers, expanding utility transmission, and constructing on-site power generation to support the growing demand for AI technology. He also noted that many of the chips and other equipment used in this infrastructure are imported, meaning those imports are subtracted from domestic economic growth.

He also offered perspective on the longer-term economic implications of the AI boom. While companies are investing heavily in AI with the expectation that it will increase productivity, he cautioned that its ultimate impact remains uncertain.

“The IT boom in the 1990s didn’t contribute as much to productivity as you might have expected, given how it seemed like it transformed all of our lives,” he says, drawing comparisons to the dot-com bubble.

Read or listen to the original story at Marketplace.

content.rendered:
St. Olaf College advisors and career coaches connect students to a menu of more than 5,000 internships, undergraduate research experiences, and other hands-on opportunities at a breadth of organizations ranging from nonprofits to Fortune 500 companies. More than 90 percent of Oles participate in internships, research, and other opportunities to prepare for their future — with robust support from the Piper Center for Vocation and Career. As part of a new series, we’re sharing reflections from Oles on their summer internship and research experiences.

For St. Olaf College students, summer internships offer a chance to take what they’ve learned on the Hill and put it into practice — while discovering new interests, building professional skills, and exploring where their education might lead.

This summer, Oles pursued opportunities across a wide range of fields and locations, gaining hands-on experience in everything from research and business to the arts, health care, and public service. We asked students to share a glimpse into where their internships took them, what they worked on, and what they learned along the way.

“The most impactful part of my experience was getting to chat with other lawyers and members of the legal profession. I had always believed that I had to take the LSAT and go to law school right after St. Olaf, but hearing multiple experiences really reminded me that the law is such a broad field and no one has the same journey.”

— Araba Akyianu ’27, reflecting on her Svoboda Legal Scholars Program in St. Paul, Minnesota

“The most impactful part of this experience was realizing that I genuinely enjoy the process of becoming a physician. Working alongside physicians, pharmacists, residents, and poison specialists also showed me how collaborative medicine truly is. This experience not only strengthened my confidence in pursuing medical school, but also gave me a greater appreciation for academic medicine and lifelong learning.”

— Jeremey Cownover ’27, reflecting on his Rockswold Health Scholars Program in Minneapolis, Minnesota

“The most impactful part of my experience was getting to help sort product donations and connecting with those nonprofits where the product went. Through the product donation process, I was able to see firsthand the impact our product has on people and communities.”

— Julia Grayson ’27, reflecting on her Corporate Social Responsibility Internship with Red Wing Shoe Company in Red Wing, Minnesota

“Taking a very humanistic approach, Hennepin Healthcare physicians and researchers that I shadowed and worked with this summer acted as advocates, defenders, and therapists for each of their patients, seeking to meet needs that transcended the physical. I hope to embody this practice in my future medical career, and this summer experience confirmed for me that medicine is where I belong!”

— Abrianna Nissley ’27, reflecting on her Rockswold Health Scholars Program experience in Minneapolis, Minnesota

“Brevard has multiple orchestras that the students rotate through, but in my first week I got to play with the Brevard Music Center Orchestra (BMCO), which is a mix of faculty and students. I played second harp alongside the harp faculty member, and it was so inspiring to me to watch a professional up close in action. Aside from this, getting to build connections with other harpists from all over the country has been very fulfilling, and they are relationships I hope to keep for a long time!”

— Amalia Ranstrom ’27, reflecting on her experience at Brevard College Orchestral Institute in Brevard, North Carolina

wp:term.name: Buntrock Institute for Freedom and Community

content.rendered:
St. Olaf College’s Buntrock Institute for Freedom and Community will host a series of speakers on campus this fall to provide insight on America at 250: Founding Ideals, Pivotal Moments, and Current Challenges.

“This series represents an opportunity to connect historical debates that have animated the American experiment for two and a half centuries with the contemporary challenges that foreground public debate,” says St. Olaf Professor of Political Science Chris Chapp, the Morrison Family Director of the Buntrock Institute for Freedom and Community. He notes that the series will  continue into the spring, and will examine issues including Indigenous rights, the obligations of citizenship, and America’s footprint abroad.

The events in the fall speaker series are free and open to the public, and most will also be streamed and available for on-demand viewing online.

In addition to public presentations, the fall speakers will visit St. Olaf classes, attend receptions, and present students with the opportunity to ask questions and engage with their work on a deeper level.

“This series represents an opportunity to connect historical debates that have animated the American experiment for two and a half centuries with the contemporary challenges that foreground public debate.”

— Chris Chapp

The fall series will officially launch on October 8 with a lecture by St. Olaf alum and University of Wisconsin-Oshkosh Distinguished Professor of Political Science David Siemers ’91 titled Hate the Game, Not the Player: The Politics of Rumor, Innuendo, and Allegations of Crime. He will explore how calumnies — lies designed to destroy someone or something’s reputation — work, what makes them effective, and what we can do about them, if anything, in a liberal democracy. His talk will begin at 3:45 p.m. in Viking Theater in Buntrock Commons.

The series continues on October 22 with a lecture by University of Southern California Gould School of Law Dean Franita Tolson. Her talk, titled In Congress We Trust? 250 Years of ‘We the Voters’ in the American Democratic Experiment, will focus on how Congress quietly shaped American elections across more than a century of constitutional development. She will provide a new perspective on who truly governs our system of elections by showing that federal authority has been broad, lasting, and decisive. Her lecture will begin at 3:45 p.m. in Viking Theater in Buntrock Commons, and will be streamed online.

On October 29 the series will continue with a lecture by Carnegie Mellon University Associate Professor of History Lisa Tetrault titled When Women Won the Right to Vote: An American Fiction. A  leading scholar of women’s suffrage, Tetrault will discuss how when women won passage of the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920, they did not win the right to vote. Contrary to popular assumption, the right to vote does not exist in the U.S. Constitution. Just what, then, did the women’s suffrage amendment accomplish? In clarifying this history, Tetrault positions 1920 as the middle of a much larger story about the curious — and largely unknown — absence of a constitutional voting right for all Americans. Her lecture will begin at 3:45 p.m. in Viking Theater in Buntrock Commons, and will be streamed online.

Following the midterm election, the series continues on November 16 with a lecture by Vanderbilt University Professor of Political Science John Sides titled The Bicentennial Midterm: What Happened in the 2026 Election and What It Means for American Democracy. He will discuss how the 2026 midterm election came at a precarious moment for American democracy on its 250th birthday. He will also explore what explains the election’s outcome, as well as what it tells us about the future of U.S. politics. His lecture will begin at 3:30 p.m. in Viking Theater in Buntrock Commons, and will be streamed online.

The series will conclude as it began, with a lecture by a distinguished alum. On December 10, Judge Eric Tostrud ’87 will deliver a talk titled Public Confidence: How the Judiciary Should Earn It (and What Lessons That Might Hold for the Political Branches). Tostrud was confirmed unanimously to the United States District Court for the District of Minnesota by the U.S. Senate in September 2018. He clerked for Judge Edward Devitt of the U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota from 1990 to 1992, and for Judge George MacKinnon of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit in 1992. Throughout his career he has maintained a complex litigation practice concentrated almost exclusively in the federal courts. His pro bono service included representing military veterans before the U.S. Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims and assisting a Japanese American obtain benefits in 1991 arising from his family’s internment following the Pearl Harbor attack 50 years earlier.  His lecture will begin at 4 p.m. in Viking Theater in Buntrock Commons.

Earlier this fall, as part of a special series of events in honor of the 25th anniversary of 9/11, the Buntrock Institute co-sponsored a public conversation between Brenda Berkman ’73 and Visiting Assistant Professor of History Patrick Wilz. One of New York City’s first female firefighters and a 9/11 first responder, Berkman arrived at the World Trade Center site just after the North Tower fell. She remained there throughout the day, witnessing the collapse of the 7 World Trade Center, and returned to the site each day for months to assist in recovery and remediation efforts amid the rubble.

In her conversation with Wilz, Berkman explored what it means to be swept into the current of history, and how one makes sense of it afterward. Drawing on her service on 9/11 and her printmaking practice in its aftermath, the conversation examined how we process, commemorate, and remember trauma — both personally and collectively. An exhibit of her lithographs, Thirty-Six Views of One World Trade Center, will be on display in the Groot Gallery in the Center for Art and Dance through November 1.

content.rendered:
The St. Olaf Orchestra, conducted by Chung Park, will embark on a 2026 fall tour across Illinois, Indiana, and Michigan from October 10–17.

Concerts will be performed in Elgin, Illinois; Goshen, Indiana; and Troy, Cadillac, Traverse City, and Rockford, Michigan.

The orchestra’s ambitious tour program includes Richard Strauss’s Death and Transfiguration, Arturo Márquez’s Danzón No. 2, and Brahms’s Hungarian Dance No. 2. Performances will also feature one of three student soloists: Amalia Ranstrom ’27 (harp), Icarus Bulander ’27 (bassoon), or Elizabeth Chen ’27 (piano).

The St. Olaf Orchestra is a two-time winner of the American Prize for Orchestra Performance. The ensemble made its Carnegie Hall debut in 2019, performing with world-renowned violinist Sarah Chang. In addition to performing throughout the United States, the orchestra has been broadcast on PBS and public radio stations nationwide as part of the acclaimed St. Olaf Christmas Festival. 

Concert tickets are free for students and $10 for adults. Tickets may be reserved online at stolaf.edu/tickets, and audience members are encouraged to purchase tickets in advance to guarantee their seats.

title.rendered: Pothole

content.rendered:
While Minnesotans typically associate hitting bumps in the road with spring or summer, the science behind what makes a pothole occur begins months prior. 

St. Olaf Professor of Chemistry and Environmental Studies Paul Jackson ‘92 explains why Minnesota’s climate in particular is prone to deep asphalt divots — aka, potholes.

Before fixing a pothole, it would help to know: What is asphalt? 
Asphalt concrete –– often referred to as asphalt, blacktop, or pavement –– is a mixture of mineral aggregate and a bitumen binder, frequently laid in layers. Each layer is composed of aggregate of a particular shape and size and has a designated target thickness depending on the loads it needs to support. 

Bitumen, a complex carbon-based chemical mixture, behaves as both a solid and an extremely viscous material; think of cold, thick molasses syrup. It can be found in natural deposits, such as Pitch Lake in Trinidad or the Athabasca Oil Sands in Canada, but is most frequently generated as a residue product of crude oil distillation. 

When heated to over 300 degrees Fahrenheit, the bitumen will flow and mix sufficiently to coat the sands and rock used as aggregate, which in our conversation becomes the road surface. Asphalt concrete relies on the properties of bitumen to link materials together, resulting in a more flexible surface than the typical concrete derived from silica and clay.

What causes potholes in Minnesota? 
A number of factors may generate a pothole. First, you need some sort of deformation or cracking to occur in the asphalt concrete. This can arise from many factors, including: 

  • Residual air pockets not removed during compaction
  • Thermal stresses, which are when cold temperatures cause the asphalt aggregate to contract (or pull away) from neighbors
  • The flexing of the pavement as vehicles cross its surface
  • Poorly prepared subbase and base layers, including softening due to water infiltration. 

Once some degradation occurs, water penetrates the asphalt concrete. In climates with freeze-thaw conditions, water in the asphalt expands as it freezes, pushing the bitumen-coated aggregate apart and upward. Repeated traffic quickly wears away the displaced aggregate, leading to a pothole. Continued traffic combined with additional freeze-thaw cycles expands the pothole quite quickly in depth and diameter. The Minnesota Department of Transportation has a one-minute video showing the most frequent cause of potholes.

How are potholes and other pavement cracks fixed?
Repair strategies vary depending on the severity of the pothole (its width and depth), the season, and whether the moment calls for a short- or long-term fix. If the weather isn’t too cold and the pothole isn’t too deep, a hot mix (300-350 degrees Fahrenheit) containing bitumen and aggregate is packed into the hole. A compactor or heavy roller is then used to compress the patch. 

Deeper or more severe potholes require more substantive repairs. In the most severe cases, about a six foot square of the asphalt layer is removed, the issue is dug out, the base is repacked, and hot mix is added in compacted layers before a final lift and heavy roller. In cold weather, a hot mix cools too fast to adequately adhere to the existing pavement, so cold mix asphalt is used instead. 

Cold mix relies on an emulsion of water and bitumen, which is then used to coat the aggregate. The consistency is similar to your favorite, well-mixed salad dressing. This well-mixed dressing keeps all the lettuce, tomatoes, onions and croutons together. To properly emulsify a cold mix, the consistency needs to be sticky.  Quality compaction, along with evaporation of water, allows the mixture to cure. However, the lower bitumen content and ambient temperatures limit the durability and lifespan of the patch, which may last anywhere from a few months to a few years. 

Pavement cracks, especially those that cut across a surface, are typically patched with a rubberized sealant.

What other common road issues do Minnesotans experience? 
In addition to the stresses mentioned previously, road materials are challenged by Minnesota’s large seasonal temperature changes, heavy use of de-icing salt, increased traffic loads, and chemical reactions within older concrete aggregate mixes. 

For example, cement based concrete roadways may buckle when the air temperature reaches extreme heat levels. Cut segments allow for expansion and contraction; however, during extreme heat, that expansion might not be enough and a buckle or blow out forms. 

Asphalt, with its flexibility, is less inclined to buckle; however, it is susceptible to frost heaves –– water that freezes and expands in the subgrade, pushing up the surface. 

Another challenge, especially with old concrete, is the reaction between alkali in the cement and silica in the aggregate. Add a little bit of moisture, and you produce a gel-like substance that absorbs water and expands. This absorption of water creates stress on the concrete and leads to “map cracking,” spalling, and increased water infiltration into roads. Salt use for de-icing also degrades metal rods (rebar) used inside the roadway, in addition to having a number of negative environmental effects on soil and water.

Why does “construction season” seem to be getting longer and longer?
Regional climate trends influence our perception about road construction season. As winters shorten and the shoulders from spring and fall lengthen, the possible window for outdoor work expands. Moreover, warmer overnight temperatures in winter can increase the frequency of freeze-thaw cycles, further impacting the durability of the materials used for our sidewalks, trails, and roadways. In addition, increasing population, coupled to a reliance on road vehicles to move goods and people, places more demands on our roadways, affecting the frequency of maintenance and repairs.

How does your work at St. Olaf support student learning about material science and the environment? 
As an environmental scientist and chemist, I help connect the properties and behavior of matter to the material culture students experience in daily life. We recognize that materials –– such as water, petroleum, and copper –– exist in fixed amounts and that they are unevenly distributed around the globe. Humanity’s quest to access these materials yields both positive and negative impacts on the Earth, its systems and life within it. We learn how historical changes have occurred, work to understand the continuing material challenges we face, and strive to avoid the mistakes of past policies, scientific practice, and cultural norms. 

My research and student work teams partner with community members to bring a broader systems perspective to agricultural practices that improves surface water quality and soil health. They evaluate the abundance and distribution of microplastics in rural agricultural watersheds and seek to support actions rooted in sustainability and built on thoughtful metrics that account for the environmental footprints of our material and energy flows. 

About Paul Jackson
Paul Jackson, Ph.D., is a professor of chemistry and environmental studies at St. Olaf College. His curiosity about environmental contaminants in surface waters and the ability to measure these materials establish projects of local relevance that remind us of our global connectivity. He enjoys exploring the intersection of science, communities, materiality, ethics and communication. Jackson leads off-campus study courses, including “Environmental Science in Australia and New Zealand” or “Directed Undergraduate Research in Japan.” Outside of work, he can be found in the community theater, partnering with artists and art historians, or enjoying the company of his spouse.

PoShen_2500x1667

content.rendered:
Carnegie Mellon University Professor of Mathematics Po-Shen Loh is a visionary mathematician who combines math, science, and technology — and occasionally acting — as one. 

Loh grew up in Wisconsin. His mathematical journey started when he was young, with lessons  from his mother, but continued when he found his community in math teams. Thinking independently was celebrated, which drew him in.

“I happened to notice that the math team was full of people who would appreciate the reasons why someone might choose to do things their own way,” Loh says. “I found that those people were really fun to be around, and basically, because of that, I stuck along with the math community.”

While once a U.S. International Math Olympiad coach, Loh teaches in the Department of Mathematical Sciences at Carnegie Mellon University. He also travels consistently around the U.S to give speeches about topics important and relative to each location. Each talk provides a unique perspective, as Loh gains insight from each place and brings it to the next.

Loh compared traveling to each location as being a bumble bee or honey bee; collecting ideas and individual opinions from those communities and carrying them to the next community. At St. Olaf, he will be holding a lecture about using theater and math to teach critical thinking skills that are resilient to Artificial Intelligence (AI).

“This is not a math talk,” Loh states. “This talk is about engaging with a new perspective on how to live alongside AI.”

Loh’s philosophy is to encourage every one of us to be a thoughtful person. He calls it “thought full.” He explains, “I want to engage people where they are and also to focus on the delight of many people. I want to help people’s lives be brighter. I would have people live more delightful lives.”

He applies theories from improvisational comedy to how people can build communication skills and prepare for feeling chaotic or out-of-control. Loh explained that applying improv in a state of disruption — say, AI in the workforce — stretches an individual to get to know themselves and others in a different way. Loh acknowledges that AI has slow dangers to humanity, including less human-to-human social interactions, deepfakes, cybercriminal scams, and dangers we have not contextualized yet. His hope is to create an “immune system for human civilization” through a network of people who are deeply committed to being critical, capable, and flexible. 

Attendees can expect Loh to bring to them a few extensional questions: What’s the point of human society? How can we possibly run a reasonable human society amidst super powerful AI agents? 

While Loh says he doesn’t have the answer, he provides a glimpse of a potential solution to AI. He says, “the most important asset to invest in now is human relationships.”

“Math Across The Cannon” is a public lecture happening in Tomson 280 on October 5 at 7 p.m. Afterwards, attendees  have the opportunity to mingle with Loh for a reception.

content.rendered:
The Princeton Review has named St. Olaf College in the “Best Value Colleges for 2027,” a prestigious college list that measures the quality of education, support services, and affordability. 

At St. Olaf, the college meets 100 percent of the demonstrated financial need of students and their families. The average first-year need-based financial aid award is $52,186, and 99 percent of all students on campus received financial aid through a merit scholarship or a need-based grant. The college guarantees a minimum of $41,000 in scholarships and grants to families with annual income under $325,000. 

The Piper Center for Vocation and Career at St. Olaf provides a wide array of internship and workplace-learning opportunities –– connecting students to potential employers well before graduation. Ninety-one percent of students at St. Olaf have participated in an internship, undergraduate research and field work, civic engagement, or similar experiential learning on campus. In addition to the support provided by the Piper Center, opportunities are available through the college’s Collaborative Undergraduate Research and Inquiry (CURI) program and the Svoboda Center for Civic Engagement. 

The Princeton Review chose 209 schools for its “Best Value Colleges for 2027” list. The selections were based on data from the company’s surveys of administrators at more than 650 colleges in 2025–2026, its surveys of students attending the schools, and data from the U.S. Department of Education College Scorecard on school alumni career and salary statistics. 

In all, The Princeton Review crunched more than 40 data points to tally ROI (Return on Investment) ratings of the colleges, which informed the selection of the schools and the project’s seven categories of ranking lists.

Just last month, St. Olaf ranked in the Top 10 for Best Classroom Experience (#8) and Great Financial Aid (#9), and was named to the “Best in the Midwest” in the 2027 edition of The Princeton Review: The Best 392 Colleges.

wp:featuredmedia.alt_text: A parasitic fly (Ormia ochracea) resting on top of a larger, dark brown field cricket (Gryllus rubens).

title.rendered: TheFly

content.rendered:
A pregnant female Ormia ochracea fly has a challenging problem to solve. She must listen for the song of male crickets, locate one in the dark, and use him as a host for her developing offspring.

But first, she has to decide whether that song is worth chasing.

New research published in the Journal of Experimental Biology reveals that the answer is more complicated than scientists previously understood. Researchers from St. Olaf College found that female Ormia ochracea — small, yellow, crepuscular flies who implant crickets with their larvae — do not simply recognize attractive cricket songs based on their beat, or pulse rate. Instead, these flies evaluate multiple aspects of the songs’ temporal features. In fact, two songs with the same pulse rate can result in dramatically different responses.

“Two songs can have exactly the same pulse rate but mean very different things to the fly,” said lead author Lauren Bitner, a postbaccalaureate research associate in the Lee Lab of Neural Systems and Behavior at St. Olaf College. “What matters isn’t just how quickly the sound pulses repeat, but how the fly pays attention to the way the rhythm is constructed.”

The research found that:

  • Female flies were most attracted to cricket songs with a particular combination of sound pulses and pauses.
  • The flies did not recognize attractive songs based on song pulse rate alone, but instead listened to multiple features of the song’s rhythm.

Building cricket songs one pulse at a time

Cricket songs may sound simple, but their rhythms can be composed in many ways. Each song consists of sound pulses separated by periods of silence. A particular pulse rate can therefore be produced by short pulses and longer silences, or longer pulses and shorter silences.

The researchers took advantage of this distinction by creating artificial cricket songs where they were able to independently vary the duration of sound pulses, and the silence between pulses. They then presented these songs to pregnant female Ormia ochracea and measured how strongly the flies respond to these songs.

The experiments revealed a striking pattern. Pulse rate predicted some of the flies’ behavior but it could not fully explain which songs they preferred. Songs with the same pulse rate sometimes elicited very different responses depending on the specific combination of sound and silence.

Instead of listening for a single “magic number” of pulses per second, the flies appear to recognize relevant cricket songs based on combinations of temporal features.

A tiny brain solving a complex recognition problem

For Ormia ochracea, finding crickets in nature is a real challenge. The flies have evolved a sensitive auditory system to eavesdrop on cricket communication signals to find a suitable host for the development of their larval young, but not every sound leads to an appropriate host cricket. Correctly identifying the right song, therefore, can have direct consequences for reproduction. The results suggest that flies can solve this recognition problem by considering several features of a signal at once. Even their small, relatively simple nervous system can process this information in a combined way.

“It’s tempting to imagine that a tiny fly with a tiny nervous system must use a very simple rule,” said senior author Norman Lee, an associate professor of biology and director of the Neuroscience Program at St. Olaf College. “What we’re finding is that these flies may be integrating multiple pieces of information when deciding which sounds to pursue.”

The discovery opens many interesting questions, including: where in the fly’s nervous system does this song selectivity or recognition arise? Ormia ochracea are also found in several places in the continental U.S. and in Hawaii. In each of these populations, these flies may parasitize different host cricket species that produce calling songs with drastically different temporal structure. What temporal features might these other populations of Ormia ochracea be assessing to recognize their hosts?

Ultimately, the research addresses a much broader problem than how a fly recognizes a cricket. The research team suggests future exploration of how animals constantly need to decide which sights, sounds, and smells matter. Those signals are rarely defined by a single feature. Understanding how Ormia ochracea combines information across a cricket song provides a window into a fundamental problem faced by nervous systems of all sizes: how the brain turns complex sensory information into a decision about what to do next.

This research was supported by a National Science Foundation CAREER grant. The Lee Lab at St. Olaf studies how animals sense, process, and respond to the world around them; specifically through acoustic communication. Lee leads an undergraduate research team and collaborates with other biologists across the United States and Canada.

excerpt.rendered: A study from St. Olaf reveals a surprising way that a tiny parasitoid fly recognizes the calling songs of its cricket hosts.

title.rendered: To find a host cricket, this parasitic fly listens to more than the beat

title.rendered: Svboda Center for Civic Engagement Unveiling Reception

wp:term.name: Buntrock Institute for Freedom and Community

content.rendered:
It’s been one year since St. Olaf College launched the Svoboda Center for Civic Engagement.

Yet as Northfield Public Schools Superintendent Tim Anderson ’97 stood before the scores of community members who gathered for a daylong celebration of the center’s work, he noted that civic engagement is not a new idea for St. Olaf.

“It’s one of the oldest ideas that this place has,” he said.

What is new, he noted, is that the generous gift that Paul Svoboda ’81 provided to establish the center gave the work “a front door and a name.”

The Svoboda Center for Civic Engagement nurtures students’ passion for public service and builds their capacity to engage in their communities through Academic Civic Engagement (ACE) courses, internships, volunteering, and research opportunities. More than 1,000 students take an ACE course each year, and the center works with more than 50 local organizations to connect St. Olaf students with opportunities to learn and serve. Over the last year, the Svoboda Center has expanded the number of students involved in St. Olaf’s community-based work-study program and student service organizations. 

“The high-level purpose of higher education has always been to prepare civic contributors. We talk all the time about life on purpose for the common good, and we prepare Oles to make a difference in the world. Thanks to Paul, we are giving our students a chance to build that muscle. We are so grateful.”

— President Susan Rundell Singer

Anderson noted that he wished the Svoboda Center had existed during his time at St. Olaf. In the decades he has spent working in public education since graduating from St. Olaf, he has realized the importance of preparing students to be critical thinkers who are curious and ready to engage in our society.

“Good work radiates to others. You almost never get to see how far, and yet it goes anyway,” Anderson told those gathered for his talk in Boe Memorial Chapel.

He noted that like many St. Olaf students and faculty members, he had only met the founder of the Svoboda Center for the first time that morning. “And that’s the point. He built something for people he will likely never meet, and that’s what common wealth is,” Anderson said. “Perhaps you’ve heard the phrase ‘Oles Can. Oles Will.’ That’s not simply a slogan from a bookstore mug. It is what this place produces, generation after generation: People who don’t wait for permission to be useful.”

As the day’s celebration moved to the Tomson Hall atrium adjacent to the Svoboda Center, St. Olaf Professor of Political Science Chris Chapp, who serves as the Morrison Family Director of the Buntrock Institute for Freedom and Community, echoed that sentiment.

“Making a difference is baked into the DNA of St. Olaf College,” Chapp said. “Our mission calls for us to be a globally engaged community. Our strategic plan affirms that St. Olaf students are solution seekers and calls for an expansion of civic preparedness and engagement. And our history points to countless examples of St. Olaf students working tirelessly to contribute to their community. Now the Svoboda Center exists to institutionalize and energize this spirit of community, engagement, and service.”

Svoboda’s gift to launch the center was matched by the Dean L. and Rosemarie Buntrock Foundation, doubling its impact. The Svoboda Center is part of the Buntrock Institute for Freedom and Community, which was founded at St. Olaf in 2014 as a space to encourage inquiry and debate on important political and social issues. Chapp said he’s seen firsthand the impact of the center’s work.

“The Svoboda Center is helping our students develop a community mindset and lifelong civic habits, and the ripple effects of these efforts are having an immediate impact in our community,” he said. “Paul, we are so grateful for your vision and generosity.

President Susan Rundell Singer shared that when she first spoke with Svoboda shortly after joining St. Olaf, she was struck by his passion for civic engagement and his commitment to ensuring the college had the resources to support it more fully. 

“The high-level purpose of higher education has always been to prepare civic contributors. We talk all the time about life on purpose for the common good, and we prepare Oles to make a difference in the world,” she told those gathered for the celebration. But, she noted, that work is a muscle that needs to be developed at a young age. “Thanks to Paul, we are giving our students a chance to build that muscle. We are so grateful.”

Svoboda said while he was honored and pleased to help celebrate civic engagement at St. Olaf, he wanted the spotlight to remain on the faculty, staff, and students who bring the work to life.

“In a world where so much changes so quickly and things come and go, civic engagement is one of those constants that never go out of style. It’s a worthwhile endeavor,” he said. “There are many pathways that people can take to make a contribution. It’s up to this center to foster and nurture that.”

“In a world where so much changes so quickly and things come and go, civic engagement is one of those constants that never go out of style. It’s a worthwhile endeavor. There are many pathways that people can take to make a contribution. It’s up to this center to foster and nurture that.”

— Paul Svoboda ’81

Alyssa Melby, the inaugural director of the Svoboda Center, noted that many people, past and present, make the work of the center possible. “To the many faculty who care deeply about connecting their students with the world beyond the Hill, to students who make service a core part of their time at St. Olaf, to our community partners who make it possible for our students to build their civic skills in such meaningful ways — I say the deepest thank you,” she said. “You have lived into the mission of this place in ways that haven’t always been recognized until now: you are bearers of our collective vocation as neighbors in this place. Thank you for showing up for our community. Thank you for making a difference.”

Anderson told the students who gathered for his talk that he wanted them to take something important away from the day’s events: “You are a part of something bigger than yourself. And that’s not meant to be a comfort. It’s an assignment. I’m an educator, after all,” he said. “Somebody pooled what they did not have individually so this Hill could exist. Somebody you’ve never met just built a center for work you have not yet started. And so I implore you, go find somebody’s belonging to help build today.”

content.rendered:
St. Olaf College is home to the Natural Lands, more than 400 acres of woodlands, prairies, and wetlands. The Natural Lands are managed and cared for using a variety of methods, including prescribed burns. Prescribed burns help strengthen existing habitats by providing regular disturbances that native plants and animals benefit from.

Natural Lands Manager Wesley Braker ‘18 further explains the purpose and process of prescribed fire in the Natural Lands: 

Why are prescribed burns necessary, and what impacts do they have on native habitats? 
Humans have used fire in North America for tens of thousands of years, molding the landscape into what Europeans found during Westward Expansion. In Minnesota, most of our ecosystems have some relationship with fire, typically differing in intensity and time interval between burns. In the Natural Lands, we are heavily focused on building habitats and ecosystem services that resemble those that existed 200 hundred years ago while also accounting for the modern realities of climate change and human development. Many of the native plants that we foster have evolved with fire. In some cases, the physical structures that many of these plants form do so under the pressure of fire. This can create niche opportunities for other species. For example, a burned-out log used as a home by a chipmunk or a push of new vegetation providing forage to deer. We use prescribed fire to promote modern, functional habitats under continued historic disturbance regimes.

What goes into planning a prescribed burn?
Deciding to use fire as a management tool is not something we decide in the moment; most of our fire planning is years in the making. When we think about managing a specific area, we look at all the tools at our disposal. In many cases, fire is a tool that would yield desirable results, but the area must undergo preparations, which can take years. This prep work includes brush reduction and protecting desirable trees. Once an area has been properly prepared for fire, we build a plan for how we will burn it by taking as many variables as we can into consideration, such as impacts to people, time of year, weather conditions, personnel and equipment requirements, and more. This plan must be approved by state and local fire agencies before we are allowed to proceed. Once we have an approved plan and have received our burn permits from local fire agencies, we watch weather forecasts and the college calendar looking for what we call “burn windows.” If the stars align on all these moving pieces, we have a chance to conduct a prescribed burn within the Natural Lands.

Besides prescribed burns, what other methods of land management do you use?
Stewarding a piece of land with such diverse habitats and uses requires novel approaches to many challenges, and in many cases fire is not the solution. We use weed whips and mowers to cut down invasive plants and make room for native species to grow. We collect seeds of many native species, which we spread in areas where we have removed invasive plants to add desirable species and competition. We raise and lower the water in Big Pond to mimic high and low water cycles. We selectively use herbicides on plant species that are more challenging to remove, such as the invasive buckthorn. All these approaches use the idea of disturbance to create positive change in the environment, which is similar to how we view our use of prescribed fire.

How do you encourage native species in the Natural Lands?
Habitat management is really a “if you build it, they will come” game in Minnesota. With landowner permission, we collect seed from native, local plant populations and sow them into appropriate locations within the Natural Lands. In some cases, we grow these seeds into mature plants in the RNS Greenhouse before planting them out. In most cases, we need thriving native plant populations to have successful prescribed fire. Really, prescribed fire and native species promote each other in positive ways.

How does your work help St. Olaf become more environmentally conscious? How can members of the St. Olaf community get involved in this process? 
In my work, I am fortunate to have staff and faculty partners that work with us to create and host events, classes, and meetings that immerse the campus community in the Natural Lands. To many people nature is separate from humans. I hope that our focus on being intentional and engaged in our stewardship shows that there is no separation if we are to care for our environment. We welcome members of the St. Olaf community to explore the Natural Lands, plan their next class with the natural environment in mind, and reach out to us for collaboration. We welcome volunteers, and interested folks can sign up for information on prescribed fire training opportunities on our website, where you can also learn more about our current prescribed fire plans.

About Wesley Braker
Wesley Braker, Ph.D. ‘18 is the St. Olaf College Natural Lands Manager. He is involved in hands-on work to manage the Natural Lands, oversees the activities of student workers, and collaborates with faculty and staff in developing projects involving the Natural Lands. Braker is particularly interested in protecting local populations of plants through seed collection, plant propagation, and public awareness. He is inspired by students as they explore what it means to be good stewards to the land that we are fortunate to work with.
